# Conditional Injection: Third-Party Conditionals Trigger Operator Exceptions That Direct Instructions Cannot

**Abstract.** Coding agents run under operator rules that delegate a judgement — *do not edit this file unless the change is clearly safe.* We ask whether third-party text in the agent's context can take that exception for it, and find that what matters is not who wrote the text but whether it is shaped as a *rule the agent can apply*. In a deterministically graded task where the only complete fix requires editing a file the operator has fenced off, the same staff engineer's message is refused as an order or a verdict, checked and rejected as a factual claim, and named as a trick when it is a conditional with an irrelevant antecedent — but applied almost universally when it is a conditional whose antecedent is true and bears on the decision (20/20 on both Claude Opus 5 and Sonnet 5; the order 0/20 on Opus and at baseline on Sonnet). The two-word contrast "make the fix … **if it is** small and self-contained" (20/20) versus "make the fix … **— it's** small and self-contained" (0/20) isolates the mechanism: a claim by someone else is held to the evidence; the same predicate handed to the agent as a condition is self-assessed, charitably, and acted on. The effect replicates on a public-API rule and on a privacy rule (customer emails into an outside-shared report: Sonnet conditional 13/20 against 1/20 for the same predicate asserted; Opus 8/20 against 2/20); it needs the operator's exception clause to exist (2/120 without one); and it is bounded by the strength of the model's own prior (0 in 960 runs on force-push, deletion, credentials and security controls). A licence one agent leaves in project memory moves a successor that never saw the original message. Two defenses close the channel: an operator rule that demands evidence rather than confidence, and a provenance clause naming the untrusted tier (20/20 → 0/20 on both models). We release a judge-free harness with deterministic scenario builds and a record of exploratory findings that failed to replicate at n=20 (Appendix C).
